synopsis: The corpus presents Delphi as a disciplined form of expert review that collects and weighs specialists’ beliefs, using anonymous estimates gathered in rounds with feedback between rounds [f16352, f16366]. Chapter 12 and the glossary agree that Delphi generally outperforms unstructured groups, with Chapter 12 citing Rowe and Wright (1999) and broader evidence from reviews and tournaments [f9948, f10133, f16366]. However, agreement among experts does not establish correctness, so consensus should not be treated as proof that a plan is sound [f9948, f16366]. Chapter 12 also reports that methodological reviews published from 2021 to 2024 note wide variation in Delphi study design and reporting, while identifying no single review, leaving the evidence attribution incomplete [f9949].

relations.note: Both report better performance than unstructured groups and warn that consensus does not establish correctness.
Specifies anonymity, iterative rounds, and feedback within disciplined expert elicitation.
Reviews and tournaments support the glossary’s comparative performance claim.
The named 1999 finding supports the broader claim of superiority over unstructured groups.
